quantities.label: Quantities
quantities.when: to describe amount, proportion or degree

phrases.connector: …, so it is fair to say that …
…, which shows that …, and as a result …

tasks.question: How many young people do you think use social media every day?

cues.cue: teenagers / use / social media daily
models: The vast majority of teenagers use social media every day, which suggests that it has become part of daily routine, and therefore concerns about screen time are growing.

cues.cue: young people / check / their phones within minutes of waking up
models: A significant proportion of young people check their phones within minutes of waking up, and this means that social media is often the first thing they see each day.

cues.cue: teenagers / avoid / social media completely
models: Only a small minority of teenagers avoid social media completely, which highlights how deeply it has become embedded in youth culture.

cues.cue: young users / spend / more than three hours a day online
models: A considerable number of young users spend more than three hours a day online, so it is fair to say that social media use has become excessive for many.

cues.cue: teenagers / own / a smartphone by the age of thirteen
models: The overwhelming majority of teenagers own a smartphone by the age of thirteen, and this points to how early digital habits now begin.

cues.cue: young people / actually / limit their own screen time
models: Very few young people actually limit their own screen time, which shows that self-control alone is rarely enough, and as a result parental guidance still matters.

tasks.question: How much time do most students spend studying each week?

cues.cue: students / spend / around ten hours a week studying
models: Roughly half of students spend around ten hours a week studying, and this is significant because study habits vary widely between individuals.

cues.cue: students / admit / to studying only before exams
models: A significant proportion of students admit to studying only right before exams, and this means that consistent revision is often neglected.

cues.cue: students / follow / a strict weekly study schedule
models: Only a small minority of students follow a strict weekly study schedule, which highlights how rare disciplined planning really is.

cues.cue: students / rely / on last-minute cramming
models: A considerable number of students rely on last-minute cramming, so it is fair to say that time management remains a common challenge.

cues.cue: students / actually / review their notes every day
models: Very few students actually review their notes every day, which shows that daily revision is uncommon, and as a result information is quickly forgotten.

cues.cue: students / study / more than twenty hours a week
models: Barely any students study more than twenty hours a week, and this is telling because most manage their workload around other commitments.

tasks.question: How many people in your country prefer city life to country life?

cues.cue: people / say / they would move to the city for work
models: A considerable number of people say they would move to the city for work, so it is fair to say that job opportunities strongly influence this choice.

cues.cue: young adults / choose / cities over the countryside
models: The vast majority of young adults choose cities over the countryside, which suggests that convenience and opportunity outweigh space and quiet, and therefore cities keep growing.

cues.cue: people / say / they would prefer to retire in the countryside
models: Roughly half of people say they would prefer to retire in the countryside, and this is significant because priorities clearly shift with age.

cues.cue: people / actively / choose rural life while young
models: Only a small minority of people actively choose rural life while young, which highlights how strongly career prospects pull people towards cities.

cues.cue: city residents / say / they enjoy easy access to services
models: The overwhelming majority of city residents say they enjoy easy access to services, and this points to convenience as the main draw of urban life.

cues.cue: families / choose / to move to small villages each year
models: Only a handful of families choose to move to small villages each year, whereas the rest stay in or move to larger towns, and therefore rural populations continue to shrink.

tasks.question: How much do people rely on their phones these days?

cues.cue: people / check / their phones first thing in the morning
models: The vast majority of people check their phones first thing in the morning, which suggests that phones have become central to daily routines, and therefore many struggle to start the day without them.

cues.cue: people / admit / feeling anxious without their phone
models: A significant proportion of people admit feeling anxious without their phone nearby, and this means that dependence has become a genuine psychological issue for many.

cues.cue: adults / use / their phones for more than five hours a day
models: A considerable number of adults use their phones for more than five hours a day, so it is fair to say that screen time has crept steadily upward.

cues.cue: people / actually / turn off notifications
models: Very few people actually turn off notifications, which shows that constant alerts are widely tolerated, and as a result concentration often suffers.

cues.cue: smartphone owners / rely / on their phone for daily tasks
models: The overwhelming majority of smartphone owners rely on their phone for daily tasks like banking and navigation, and this points to how essential the device has become.

cues.cue: people / go / a full day without checking their phone
models: Barely any people go a full day without checking their phone, and this is telling because constant connectivity is now the norm rather than the exception.

tasks.question: How many people do you think will own an electric car in ten years?

cues.cue: drivers / switch / to electric
models: The overwhelming majority of drivers may soon switch to electric, and this points to a major shift in how vehicles are powered.

cues.cue: car manufacturers / plan / to sell mostly electric models
models: The vast majority of car manufacturers plan to sell mostly electric models within a decade, which suggests that the industry itself is driving the shift, and therefore petrol cars may soon become rare.

cues.cue: new car buyers / consider / an electric model
models: A significant proportion of new car buyers already consider an electric model, and this means that consumer attitudes are changing faster than expected.

cues.cue: drivers / say / they would switch if charging points were more common
models: Roughly half of drivers say they would switch to electric if charging points were more common, and this is significant because infrastructure remains the main obstacle.

cues.cue: people / still / prefer petrol cars for long journeys
models: Only a small minority of people still prefer petrol cars for long journeys, which highlights how quickly confidence in electric range has grown.

cues.cue: new charging stations / are being built / across the country
models: Countless new charging stations are being built across the country, which underlines the fact that infrastructure is expanding rapidly to meet demand.

tasks.question: How much of your day do you spend using technology?

cues.cue: people / spend / more than half their waking hours on screens
models: The vast majority of people spend more than half their waking hours on screens, which suggests that technology now dominates daily life, and therefore concerns about balance are growing.

cues.cue: people / use / technology for both work and leisure
models: A significant proportion of people use technology for both work and leisure, and this means the boundary between the two has become increasingly blurred.

cues.cue: my daily screen time / go / towards work-related tasks
models: Roughly half of my daily screen time goes towards work-related tasks, and this is significant because leisure use takes up the rest.

cues.cue: people / spend / over four hours a day on social media alone
models: A considerable number of people spend over four hours a day on social media alone, so it is fair to say that this single habit shapes much of their screen time.

cues.cue: people / actually / track how much time they spend online
models: Very few people actually track how much time they spend online, which shows that most underestimate their real usage, and as a result habits go unchecked.

cues.cue: people / spend / a whole day completely offline
models: Barely any people spend a whole day completely offline, and this is telling because being constantly connected has become the default.
